concept: LLM tells in code, commit messages, comments and READMEs
summary: Source-anchored research for LLM tells in code, commit messages, comments and READMEs. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: The characteristic narration tell is a comment that restates the adjacent code, adding maintenance burden and burying the few comments that matter. (low confidence)

Comment-based detection is a weak, proxy signal: the repository study calls its results proxy-based and warns detectors both under- and over-estimate LLM use, and other work reports commercial detectors are affected by comments and unreliable. (medium confidence)

Agent guidance for avoiding the tell: do not add comments by default; add one only for non-obvious why (rationale, constraints, invariants, trade-offs, surprising external behavior); prefer better names, types and structure over narration. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-04)
In one study of security-related AI-generated PRs, 70.4% of 2,823 commit messages were high quality (contain both Why and What) and 29.6% omitted one or both. (low confidence)

Practitioner signature list of AI-grown bloat: verbose scaffolding layers, partial fixes, ceremonial state layers mirroring other layers, non-functional placeholder subsystems left wired in, debug harness code in shipping source, and defensive abstractions that accumulate each agent turn; one Flutter app shrank 31.7% with tests passing. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-01)

The readme-ai generator emits a fixed skeleton: header with badges and logo, project introduction, features table, project structure, project index, getting started (install, usage, tests), community and contributing, license; it offers emoji theme packs prefixed to section titles. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

Wikipedia's AI-cleanup editors state the listed patterns are only potential signs of a problem, not the problem itself, and that text with these features is not necessarily AI-generated because LLMs are trained on human writing. (high confidence)

LLM comments are not uniformly poor: in a 415-comment Java evaluation, human experts judged 58.8% to match originals and 27.7% to surpass them; automated metrics such as BLEU correlated negatively with human judgment. (low confidence)

A classifier on AIDev PRs identified which of five agents (Codex, Copilot, Devin, Cursor, Claude Code) authored a PR at 97.2% F1; commit-message features dominated, with multiline commit ratio the strongest single signal (44.7% importance). (low confidence)

Per-agent signatures differ: Codex extensive multiline commits, Copilot longer PR descriptions, Cursor bullet points and hyperlinks, Devin multiline messages. Claude Code recall was only 57% in that study, so its tells are weaker. (low confidence)

Across four LLMs, generated code had on average 63.34% more code smells than reference solutions (73.35% implementation smells, 21.42% design smells), with larger increases on more complex tasks. (low confidence)

Detection tools for AI text score poorly in independent testing (all under 80% accuracy, five over 70%), so a formatting tell in a README is grounds to review, not proof of AI authorship. (medium confidence)

Search-result snippets (not fetched) report opposite security-study findings: LLM code lacking defensive constructs, and one model with error handling in only 3.3% of scripts. Excess defensiveness is not established as a general LLM tell. (low confidence)

Population-level word statistics cannot identify an individual LLM-written text, and cannot separate direct LLM use from humans unconsciously adopting LLM-preferred vocabulary; a single flagged word is weak evidence. (medium confidence)

GitClear's analysis of 211M changed lines (2020-2024) reports copy/pasted lines rising from 8.3% to 12.3% of changed lines while moved (refactored) lines fell from 25% to under 10%, read as assistants adding new code rather than reusing existing functions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-01-01)

Excess-vocabulary analysis of 15M+ PubMed abstracts found 2024 excess words were mostly style words (verbs ~66%, adjectives ~14%) such as delves, intricate, pivotal, unlike COVID-era excess words which were content nouns; it estimates at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were LLM-processed. (high confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-02)

A Stanford study of seven GPT detectors found about 61% of non-native English writers' essays flagged as AI; detectors penalise plain, predictable wording, so clean simple prose is a false-positive risk rather than a tell. (high confidence)

A 2021-2025 study of eight GitHub repositories found comments flagged as likely LLM-generated concentrated in Meta and Explanation categories, and remained relatively stable over time. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-01)

Claude Code by default appends a Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer to commit messages and a 'Generated with Claude Code' line to PR bodies; cloud sessions also add a claude.ai link. The attribution.commit, attribution.pr and attribution.sessionUrl settings change or hide them. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)
Trailer tells are easily removed (git commit --amend, force-push, commit-msg hook), so their absence does not show human authorship. (low confidence)

Agent-authored PRs show message-code inconsistency: descriptions can claim functionality with no corresponding implementation, or describe changes incompletely. A description's confident summary therefore needs checking against the diff. (medium confidence)

Agent-generated code shows procedural bloat (Long Method dominant) on simple tasks and architectural decay (God Class, superficial file separation) in complex systems; total lines of code correlates with architectural degradation at rho=0.94. (medium confidence)

More capable models can produce messier code as they try to handle every edge case, yielding excessively long methods; detailed prompts and few-shot examples did not reduce defects in that study. (low confidence)

Google's developer documentation style guide prescribes active voice, second person, conditions before instructions, and friendly-but-not-frivolous tone; these are human-authored norms that clean LLM output can also satisfy, so following them is not itself a tell. (medium confidence)

The Wikipedia guide's stronger tells are content-level: undue emphasis on significance and legacy, vague attribution ('experts argue'), 'not just X but Y' parallelism, copula avoidance, and rigid 'challenges and future prospects' sections; these signal padding, not correctness of grammar. (medium confidence)

Human judgement alone performs no better than chance at telling AI from human text per the Wikipedia guide, and writers who fear accusation may distort their style; human and LLM writing are also converging. (low confidence)

Wikipedia's AI-writing guide lists emoji used as formatting, Markdown syntax, excess boldface, vertical lists with inline headers, and skipped or heading-only-heading structures as signs of AI text, and says they are signs of a possible problem, not the problem itself. (high confidence)

LLM changelog generation can produce entries that are fluent, correctly formatted and false, such as inferring an extra change that never shipped or inventing a value like a cache TTL; the recommended control is human review of the draft. (low confidence)

The avoid-ai-writing skill (74 pattern categories, deterministic detector, CI and pre-commit integration) treats generic conclusions, chatbot artifacts and formatting inconsistencies as tells that can be linted in docs. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)
